author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The Note Below the Water
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
The empty stage made a sound.

I heard it while we were checking the lanterns along Starwake Pier. It was a low note, almost musical, vibrating through the wooden platform after a gust of wind moved across the water.

Greg stopped.

"Did you hear that?"

I nodded.

"Was that your guitar?"

He held up both hands.

"Nope."

The stage was empty. The cables had been packed away after the Listening Fair, and the repaired railings were still marked with temporary load limits. The western section had not yet reopened.

The note sounded again.

It was deeper than anything the little stage should have produced.

Greg crouched near the platform.

"That's coming from underneath."

I thought of the second bell at Tideglass.

"Can we check safely?"

He looked at the railing.

"Not from the closed section. Let's get someone who knows the structure."

We found Tamsin near the storage shed. She listened to our description, then asked us to repeat exactly where we'd stood and what the wind had been doing. She was not interested in a ghost story.

Danse arrived with a vibration meter.

Toph came because Tamsin had asked whether the stone support beneath the pier was moving.

Greg looked between them.

"I think I know what note it is."

Toph raised an eyebrow.

"That's useful, but I need to know what's making it."

"Fair."

We set up the meter on the safe platform and waited for the wind to shift.

The note came again.

Danse recorded the frequency. Toph felt the slight movement through the stone support. Tamsin checked the old service map. The measurements suggested a cavity beneath the pier was resonating when water passed through a narrow opening.

"That could be connected to the old drainage route," I said.

Danse nodded.

"Possibly. We need a water-level comparison before we say more."

Greg tapped the edge of the stage.

"It's like a guitar body. The wood makes one part of the sound, the hollow space makes another."

Toph grinned.

"Finally, the musician says something useful."

"High praise."

We laughed.

Then the wind shifted and the note grew louder.

Fen sent a warning from Tideglass. The tide was rising faster than the morning chart had predicted. The lower service passage was still sealed, and several surface drains were carrying more water than usual.

Tamsin looked at the stage.

"Close this section."

We moved the lanterns away from the western boards and posted a clear route to the upper path. Greg helped carry the equipment, checking with the volunteers rather than assigning jobs on the spot. Neri updated the public notice without listing any traveler's private destination.

The storm had not arrived yet.

That was why we had time.

Before sunset, the volunteer crew went over the evacuation plan one more time. A younger helper named Jo wanted to know whether we ought to warn everyone who lived near the water that the old tunnel was opening.

"It's not opening," Fen said from the speaking station. "The surface drains are handling the extra flow. The lower historic passage is still sealed."

Jo looked relieved, then embarrassed. "I told my brother there was a secret tunnel under the stage."

"Well," Greg said, "there might be a very boring maintenance route. I'm not volunteering to write a song about the plumbing."

I laughed, but Danse was checking the measurements with such a serious face that I stopped.

"Does the sound mean something's going to fail?" I asked.

"We don't know yet. It might mean air is moving through a cavity. It might mean the pressure is changing. The point is to observe without treating the noise as an instruction to go inside."

Tamsin recorded the warning limits and asked Jo to help point people toward the upper stairs, where the signs had been tested at eye level for several kinds of visitors. Jo said yes. There were no new volunteers sent onto the closed platform after that.

Greg pulled out his notebook. On one page he wrote the sound as a musician would hear it; on the facing page he copied the time and gauge reading from the official report. The two pages weren't interchangeable.

"Why keep them separate?" I asked.

"So nobody ends up reading my terrible chord notation as proof the pier is safe," he said.

Danse looked at the notebook.

"That is a surprisingly good control measure."

"Hey. I'm full of those."

Greg grinned, and I saw Danse's mouth almost move into a smile.

The wind made the stage sing again. Jo looked toward the boarded walkway, then returned to their post. The discipline of staying where the crew could actually help seemed as important as any discovery.

For once, I wasn't frightened by the sound simply because we didn't understand it. I was frightened in a useful way, the kind that made us ask who was responsible for the next decision.

A gust tugged at Greg's coat. He caught my hand to steady himself, then let go when the path narrowed.

"See?" he said. "No heroic rescue required."

"Not unless you plan to rescue your notebook from the rain."

He tucked it under his shirt and ran toward the shelter, laughing.

At dusk, the water rose beneath the pier. The low note sounded several times, each one a little shorter than the last. Danse marked the timing, and Greg wrote down the pitch changes in ordinary musical language.

They compared the notes.

It wasn't a perfect match to the second bell at Tideglass. The structures were different. But both sounds appeared when water pressure changed along the old service system.

"That doesn't make them the same instrument," Greg said.

"No," Danse agreed. "But it gives us a testable connection."

We sent the records to Moonroot Archive.

Severus and Neri could compare them with the damaged ledger and the older maintenance diagrams. Fen would continue monitoring the tide. Tamsin would not reopen the western pier until the supports passed the next inspection.

Nobody blamed a spirit.

Nobody pretended there wasn't danger.

After the work, Greg sat beside me on the safe bench and looked toward the dark water.

"You know what's weird?" he said.

"That the pier is singing?"

"Besides that."

I smiled.

"I used to think music was something you made when you wanted people to hear you. Today the sound was telling us something we needed to listen to."

"That's what the fair was about."

He nodded.

"Guess I finally learned my own lesson."

I leaned against him.

The air smelled of rain. The first lanterns were coming on along the safe route, and the wind carried a faint note from the old wooden supports.

Greg looked at me.

"Do you ever get scared that this place will stop being safe?"

"Yes."

"Me too."

He took my hand.

"But we know how to ask for help now. That's something."

I smiled.

He kissed my forehead.

We sat until the rain began, then walked back to the Starwake Door without crossing the closed section.

In the morning, the water had receded. The stage no longer made the note.

Tamsin recorded that too.

Greg went home and wrote a short melody based on the sound, careful to keep the work separate from the inspection report.

He played it for me that evening.

It was strange and beautiful.

"It doesn't need words," I said.

He smiled.

"No. It knows what it wants to say."

The stage remained closed.

The music didn't have to be.
